t: LeetCode 2207 - Maximize Number of Subsequences in a String: One Insertion Counted in a Single Pass
o: **Understanding the problem.** Given text and a 2-character pattern, we must insert exactly one character - either pattern[0] or pattern[1], anywhere including the ends - and maximize how often pattern appears as a subsequence afterwards. Subsequence occurrences of pattern = xy are counted by pairing each y with every x before it. In Example 1 (text = "abdcdbc", pattern = "ac") the original text already contains 2 such pairs ('a' at index 0 paired with the two c's); inserting an extra 'a' before both c's adds 2 occurrences for a total of 4, while inserting a 'c' adds only the single preceding 'a', giving 3. The constraints (text up to 10^5 characters) rule out trying every insertion position, hinting that the gain of an insertion should be computable from a couple of running counts.
k: The number of pattern occurrences equals, summed over every pattern[1] character, the count of pattern[0] characters strictly before it.

Inserting pattern[0] anywhere before all pattern[1] characters gains exactly the number of pattern[1] characters; inserting pattern[1] after all pattern[0] characters gains exactly the number of pattern[0] characters - so the answer is base + max(count0, count1).
When pattern[0] == pattern[1], add to the total before incrementing the counter so k existing copies contribute k*(k-1)/2, and the forced insertion brings it to k*(k+1)/2.

a.n: Approach 1: Try Every Insertion Position (Brute Force)
a.i: Directly emulate the statement: for each of the two pattern characters and each of the n + 1 gaps in text, build the modified string and recount subsequence occurrences from scratch. Obviously correct and hopelessly quadratic, but it validates the counting logic used later.
s: Write a helper that counts pattern-as-subsequence occurrences in any string with one scan.
For ch in {pattern[0], pattern[1]} and every gap position i, evaluate the helper on text[:i] + ch + text[i:].
a.t: O(n^2) - n + 1 insertion gaps per character, each rebuilt and recounted in O(n)
a.sp: O(n) - one materialized candidate string at a time

a.i: Scan text once tracking how many pattern[0] characters have been seen. Every pattern[1] character contributes that running count to the base total. The mandatory insertion is best spent adding pattern[0] in front (gaining count of pattern[1]) or pattern[1] at the back (gaining count of pattern[0]); both placements are realizable, so take the larger. Checking pattern[1] membership before incrementing the pattern[0] counter keeps the pattern[0]==pattern[1] case consistent.
s: For each character: if it equals pattern[1], add cnt0 to base and increment cnt1; if it equals pattern[0], increment cnt0 (this order matters when the two are equal).
a.t: O(n) - a single scan of text

w: Lead with the counting identity (each pattern[1] pairs with prior pattern[0] characters); the insertion strategy then falls out as two concrete, achievable gains. Pitfalls: the update order when pattern[0] == pattern[1] - adding the count before incrementing is what makes k copies yield k*(k-1)/2; forgetting that exactly one character must be inserted even into an empty-of-pattern text (max(cnt0, cnt1) may legitimately be based on zeros); using 32-bit totals, since counts reach n^2/4 with n = 10^5. Follow-ups: insert k characters (greedy still works - each added character gains the current opposite count), or generalize to longer patterns via DP.
